title: Function Notation: What f(x) Actually Means

scenes.title: If f(x) = 2x + 5, what does f(3) mean?
scenes.narration: Suppose a question gives f of x equals two x plus five and asks for f of three. Here is the idea: function notation is an input-output language. The three is not being multiplied by f. It tells us which input to feed into the rule. The function then produces one output from that input.

scenes.title: What does f(x) actually represent?
body: f(x) = output produced by the rule
scenes.narration: Think of the function as a machine. You put in x, the rule two x plus five acts on that input, and the result is called f of x. So f of three means use three everywhere the input variable x appears. Notice why this matters: the notation names the output; it is not ordinary multiplication notation.

scenes.title: This is where students often mix things up
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. They read the parentheses as multiplication, or they replace only part of the rule. But f of three means substitute three for every x in the function rule. If the input is negative, keep it in parentheses so the sign stays attached to the number.

scenes.title: Now evaluate the function
scenes.narration: Now calculate. Two times three is six, and six plus five is eleven. So f of three equals eleven. Each step still has meaning: three is the input, two x plus five is the rule, and eleven is the output produced by that rule.

scenes.title: Quick check: connect the notation to the graph
scenes.narration: Here is a quick verification. If f of three equals eleven, then the point three comma eleven must lie on the graph of y equals f of x. And for y equals two x plus five, plugging in x equals three gives y equals eleven, so the point checks. The big idea is simple: function notation tells you an input and asks for the output generated by the rule. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
